The Christian kingdoms built Covadonga's mythology over subsequent centuries precisely because they needed a founding miracle to frame reconquest as legitimate restoration rather than simple new conquest. Arab sources name the opposing commanders as Alqama and Munuza; the fact that those names survive suggests the engagement was at least recorded, but the scale Arab chroniclers imply is a fraction of the Frankish version.

events.label: Papal States
events.description: The strip of central Italy Pippin donated to the papacy in 756 — running from Ravenna on the Adriatic coast west to Rome — became the Papal States, the pope's own sovereign kingdom. For over eleven centuries, successive popes governed this territory as temporal rulers, appointing governors, raising armies, and waging war, until the unified Kingdom of Italy absorbed the last remnants in 1870.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Before 756, the pope was technically a subject of the Byzantine emperor, who could appoint and depose popes and override them on doctrine — a dependence the Donation ended permanently. At their largest the Papal States covered roughly a third of the Italian peninsula, including major cities like Bologna, Ferrara, and Perugia. When Italian unification abolished them in 1870, the 'Roman Question' over the pope's lost sovereignty was not formally resolved until Mussolini's Lateran Treaty in 1929, which created the Vatican City as the tiny sovereign enclave that survives today.

events.label: Charles the Bald
events.description: The youngest son of Louis the Pious, Charles the Bald ruled West Francia from 840 to 877 and briefly held the imperial title — outlasting all his brothers despite being the one whose birth triggered the original succession crisis.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Charles was a genuine patron of learning who commissioned some of the finest illuminated manuscripts of the Carolingian Renaissance, including the Bible of Vivien (c. 845), which survives and contains one of the most detailed portraits of any early medieval monarch. Despite his nickname, no contemporary source calls him bald — the epithet may have been ironic, or may refer to a territory rather than his appearance. He died in 877 near the Alps, reportedly of a fever worsened by a medication his physician administered.

events.label: Siege of Paris 885
events.description: A massive Viking fleet besieged Paris from November 885 to October 886, held off for nearly a year by Count Odo's defense of the Seine bridges — only for Emperor Charles the Fat to end the standoff by paying the Vikings 700 livres (about 257 kg) of silver and letting them plunder Burgundy instead.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The siege is unusually well documented because a monk named Abbo of Saint-Germain-des-Pres watched it from inside the walls and later wrote a Latin epic poem about it, the Bella Parisiacae urbis, which survives. One Viking leader, Sigfred, actually left earlier in the siege, satisfied with just 60 pounds of silver — a separate, smaller payoff before the main ransom. Count Odo's defense won him such prestige that when Charles the Fat was deposed, the West Frankish nobles elected Odo king, making him the first non-Carolingian king of the Franks.

events.label: End of the Carolingian Empire
events.description: Charles the Fat, the last Carolingian to hold most of the empire together, was deposed by his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia in November 887 and dead by January 888 — ending any real prospect of reversing the Verdun partition and confirming the permanent split into five successor kingdoms.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Charles briefly controlled more Carolingian territory than anyone since Charlemagne himself, inheriting the final pieces in 884 through a run of dynastic accidents. His collapse came almost entirely from the humiliation of buying off the Vikings at Paris in 886 rather than fighting them — that deal destroyed his credibility with the Frankish nobility faster than any military defeat could have. After his death, no single ruler ever held the full Carolingian inheritance again.

events.label: Henry the Fowler
events.description: Henry I the Fowler, Duke of Saxony, was elected king of East Francia in 919 — the first non-Frankish king to hold the throne — founding the Ottonian dynasty that would rule Germany for over a century and defeat the Magyar raiders who had terrorized the continent for decades.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Henry earned his nickname from a story that messengers found him fixing his birding nets when they arrived to announce he'd been elected king. He negotiated a nine-year truce with the Magyars in 924 by paying tribute — then used that pause to build fortified frontier strongholds and retrain his cavalry before crushing a Magyar invasion at the Battle of Riade in 933. He is considered the founder of the medieval German state.

events.label: Otto III in Rome
events.description: Otto III, grandson of Otto I and emperor from 996 to 1002, relocated his court to Rome and pursued an idealistic vision of a restored Christian Roman Empire — appointing his old tutor, the brilliant mathematician Gerbert of Aurillac, as Pope Sylvester II — before dying of fever at twenty-one with his project unfinished.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Otto III was fluent in Greek and Latin and had a Byzantine mother (Theophanu), which made him unusually cosmopolitan for a German king of the period. He styled himself 'Emperor of the Romans' and took the name Sylvester II for his papal appointment as a deliberate echo of Sylvester I, who had been pope during Constantine's time — the symbolism of renewing the Christian empire was entirely intentional. His early death in 1002 without an heir left the vision unrealized and returned the empire to a more conventionally German orientation under Henry II.

events.label: Gerbert of Aurillac
events.description: Gerbert of Aurillac, who became Pope Sylvester II in 999, was the most learned man in tenth-century Latin Europe — he had studied in the Christian-Muslim borderlands of Catalonia, absorbed Arabic mathematics, introduced the Hindu-Arabic numeral system and the abacus to Latin schools, and built working astronomical instruments.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gerbert is said to be the first person in Christian Europe to introduce the decimal numeral system — the Hindu-Arabic numerals (1, 2, 3...) that eventually replaced Roman numerals for calculation. He also reintroduced the armillary sphere (a physical model of the celestial spheres used to track astronomical positions) and the water organ to Latin Europe, both of which had been lost since the fall of the Western Roman Empire. His contemporaries thought him so far ahead of his time that rumors persisted he had made a pact with the devil.

events.label: Conversion of Bulgaria
events.description: Khan Boris I of Bulgaria accepted baptism from Byzantine missionaries in 864, choosing Greek Orthodox Christianity over the Latin alternative offered by Pope Nicholas I. The Bulgarian conversion brought a major Slavic state into the Byzantine cultural sphere and produced the development of the Cyrillic alphabet by the disciples of Cyril and Methodius.

events.label: Cyrillic Alphabet
events.description: The Cyrillic alphabet was developed in Bulgaria around 893 by disciples of the Byzantine missionaries Cyril and Methodius, adapting Greek letters to write Slavic sounds. It became the script of every Slavic Orthodox Christian people — Russians, Ukrainians, Bulgarians, Serbs — and is the direct reason why the Latin-Cyrillic line bisects Europe to this day.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The original alphabet Cyril himself created (around 862–863) was actually the Glagolitic script, not Cyrillic — Cyrillic was a later, simpler adaptation created by his disciples that replaced it in most places. The choice of script was inseparable from the choice of church: Latin missionaries brought the Latin alphabet, Byzantine missionaries brought Greek-derived letters; the frontier between them is still the frontier between Catholic and Orthodox Europe. The script is now used for over 50 languages across Eurasia.

events.label: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle Begins
events.description: King Alfred the Great's court began compiling the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle around 890, a year-by-year history of the English-speaking peoples written in Old English. Continuations were maintained at multiple monastic centers until the mid-twelfth century, making it the most extensive vernacular history produced anywhere in early medieval Europe.

events.label: Beowulf Composed
events.description: The Old English epic poem Beowulf, telling the story of a Geatish hero who fights the monster Grendel and a dragon, was probably composed somewhere between 700 and 1000 — the dating remains contested. Its sole surviving manuscript dates from around 1000 and survived a 1731 fire by accident. It is the longest and greatest poem in Old English.

events.label: Emergence of the Castle
events.description: The first true castles — privately owned fortified residences serving simultaneously as homes and instruments of local political control — appeared in Frankish territory in the late 9th and 10th centuries, initially as wooden towers on raised earth mounds (mottes) with a fenced courtyard (bailey) below.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The motte-and-bailey design could be built in weeks using peasant labor with no specialized engineering, making it accessible to even minor lords — and defensible enough against the hit-and-run raids Vikings favored. Stone keeps only became standard from the 11th century onward, once lords had stable enough wealth for permanent construction. Scholars estimate West Francia went from almost no private fortifications in 800 to several hundred castles by the year 1000 — the landscape of medieval Europe being literally built in real time as the Carolingian state dissolved.

events.label: Sutton Hoo Burial
events.description: An early Anglo-Saxon king, almost certainly Rædwald of East Anglia, was buried around 625 in a 90-foot ship beneath a great mound at Sutton Hoo in Suffolk. Excavated in 1939, the burial yielded the famous gilt-and-garnet helmet, gold belt buckle, sword, lyre, and Byzantine silverware — the richest find from early Anglo-Saxon England and proof of the period's vast trade connections.

events.label: Book of Kells
events.description: The Book of Kells is an illuminated Latin gospel manuscript made around 800, probably begun at Iona and completed at Kells in Ireland after Vikings forced the community to evacuate — the most spectacular surviving example of Insular (Irish-British) manuscript art, considered the pinnacle of Western calligraphy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The manuscript uses at least ten distinct pigments including lapis lazuli imported from Afghanistan, showing that even the most remote Irish monasteries were plugged into long-distance Mediterranean trade networks. The text unusually draws from both the Vulgate (Jerome's Latin Bible) and the older Vetus Latina translation, suggesting the scribes were working from multiple manuscript traditions simultaneously. The Book of Kells has been on permanent public display at Trinity College Dublin since the 1650s.

events.label: Mediterranean Long-Distance Trade
events.description: Despite the religious fault line running through the Mediterranean after the Arab conquests, long-distance trade in luxury goods — Byzantine silk, Egyptian linen, Frankish swords, Saxon slaves, Slavic furs, Baltic amber, Indian spices, African gold — continued throughout the early Middle Ages, conducted largely by Jewish, Syrian, and Italian merchants. Venice, founded in lagoons by refugees from Lombard Italy, became the principal western terminus by the tenth century.

events.label: Rise of Venice
events.description: Refugees from Lombard mainland Italy settled in the Venetian lagoon in the sixth and seventh centuries, and by the ninth and tenth centuries Venice had emerged as a self-governing maritime republic under nominal Byzantine suzerainty. By the year 1000 Venice was the dominant western trading link to Constantinople, the eastern Mediterranean, and the Islamic world.

events.label: Ulfberht Swords
events.description: Frankish smiths in the Rhineland produced exceptionally hard, well-tempered crucible-steel swords inscribed +VLFBERHT+ between roughly 800 and 1000. They were exported (often illegally — Carolingian capitularies tried to ban the trade) across northern Europe and became the most prized weapon of the Viking world; over 170 surviving examples have been catalogued.
